title: Ansel and the Colony
premise: Hazel Sandoval, a xenolinguist stationed on the forgotten colony of Meridian's Rest, discovers the settlement's children are all dreaming the same alien dream—a memory of a massacre that official records insist never happened. As she and colony administrator Ansel Voss dig into erased archives and buried testimony, they uncover that the colonial authority itself ordered the extermination of an indigenous species and rewrote history to hide it. When the corporation sends a 'reconciliation team' to silence witnesses, Hazel must choose between her duty to the linguistic mission she betrayed and the truth the children carry in their shared dreams. In the end, they broadcast the dream itself—untranslatable, undeniable—to every relay in the system, sacrificing their careers and Ansel's life to make forgetting impossible.
about_author: August Blackwood is the pen name of a former field researcher who spent six years in remote settlements before turning to fiction. They write about the people history files under 'inconsequential,' and the stories those people refuse to stop telling.

chapters.title: The Language of Dust
chapters.summary: Hazel records her daily linguistic log on Meridian's Rest, noting with quiet dread that she no longer dreams in any human language. Her POV establishes the colony's isolation and her growing estrangement from herself. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Children Who Dream Together
chapters.summary: Schoolteacher Imani reports that seven children describe an identical nightmare: red dust, screaming in a language no one taught them. Hazel interviews them, recognizing phonetic patterns from her own corrupted dreams. Emotional beat: unease curdling into wonder—and fear.

chapters.title: Ansel's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ansel Voss, the weary colony administrator, keeps unofficial records because he doesn't trust the central archive. His POV reveals he's been quietly documenting supply discrepancies—shipments that suggest something was removed from the historical record. Emotional beat: dutiful suspicion.

chapters.title: What the Archive Says
chapters.summary: Hazel requests the colony's founding records and receives a pristine, suspiciously complete file: no indigenous species ever existed here. But the children's dream-language matches fossilized vocal structures she finds in the canyon. Emotional beat: the first crack in official reality.

chapters.title: Red Dust Season
chapters.summary: A storm isolates the colony for weeks. During it, more children begin dreaming, and adults start reporting fragments too. Ansel and Hazel compare notes for the first time, forming an uneasy alliance. Emotional beat: two guarded people choosing trust.

chapters.title: The Canyon Dig
chapters.summary: Hazel leads a small expedition to the canyon and finds charred remains arranged in patterns—deliberate, organized, recent enough to deny. Ansel photographs everything before the dust can reclaim it. Emotional beat: grief arriving ahead of understanding.

chapters.title: Orders From Above
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV: a coded directive arrives from Colonial Authority instructing him to file a 'psychological contamination' report on Hazel. He stalls, realizing the corporation anticipated discovery long ago. Emotional beat: loyalty beginning to fracture along its seams.

chapters.title: Imani's Testimony
chapters.summary: Imani reveals her grandmother was a survey-team member who went silent after year one; her family letters hint at 'the clearing.' The children's dream, she argues, isn't haunting them—it's being given to them. Emotional beat: inherited guilt made personal.

chapters.title: Decoding the Dream
chapters.summary: Hazel works obsessively to translate the dream-language, discovering it encodes names—hundreds of names—of the dead. She realizes the massacre victims are speaking through the children, refusing erasure. Emotional beat: awe shadowed by horror at what communication costs.

chapters.title: The Reconciliation Team
chapters.summary: A corporate vessel arrives unannounced, carrying 'specialists' who offer generous relocation packages and ask oddly precise questions about the children. Ansel signs nothing; Hazel hides her research. Emotional beat: menace wearing a polite smile.

chapters.title: First Casualty
chapters.summary: The school burns under ambiguous circumstances, destroying Imani's classroom records. One child, Tomas, is taken 'for medical evaluation' by the team. The colony's passivity terrifies Hazel more than the act itself. Emotional beat: the cost of staying invisible.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: In the aftermath, Hazel and Ansel admit what they've become to each other—not just allies. But Ansel confesses his original orders included monitoring her, and Hazel must decide if his confession is betrayal or the truest thing she's heard. Emotional beat: intimacy built on broken ground.

chapters.title: The Erased Year
chapters.summary: Ansel breaks into the sealed administrative vault and recovers a corrupted backup: footage of the clearing operation, soldiers, and a signature—his own predecessor's, and countersigned by someone still in power. Emotional beat: vindication that feels like drowning.

chapters.title: Every Record Says Otherwise
chapters.summary: The team presents the colony with flawless documentation proving the indigenous species was mythical folklore. Half the colonists accept it gratefully. Hazel watches collective denial happen in real time. Emotional beat: the vertigo of watching truth lose gracefully.

chapters.title: Tomas Comes Home
chapters.summary: Tomas returns changed—sedated, dreamless, unable to remember the language. The other children grieve him as if he'd died. Hazel understands the team's method: not killing witnesses, but hollowing them. Emotional beat: rage refined into resolve.

chapters.title: The Broadcast Plan
chapters.summary: Hazel proposes transmitting the decoded dream—the names, the sounds, the children's testimony—on every open relay frequency during the quarterly uplink window. Ansel calculates they'll have eleven minutes before the signal is cut. Emotional beat: hope as a tactical decision.

chapters.title: Divided Colony
chapters.summary: The team offers full amnesty and off-world passage to anyone who disavows the 'massacre narrative.' Neighbors turn on neighbors; Imani is publicly denounced. Ansel must choose whether to reveal his vault evidence early. Emotional beat: a community tearing along old fault lines.

chapters.title: Eleven Minutes
chapters.summary: Uplink day. Hazel, Ansel, and the children reach the relay station under pretense of maintenance—but the team is waiting, having flipped a colonist informant. A standoff in the dust; Ansel buys time by surrendering himself. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into clarity.

chapters.title: The Names Go Out
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, inside the transmission: she broadcasts the dream entire—every name, every scream, the children singing it back in unison. Eleven minutes of the dead, sent to a million ears. The signal cuts. Silence. Then, across the system, relays begin rebroadcasting it. Emotional beat: triumph inseparable from loss.

chapters.title: What They Did to Ansel
chapters.summary: Ansel is taken aboard the corporate vessel 'for questioning.' Hazel receives a formal notice of his death by accident, plus her own termination. But the rebroadcasts won't stop, and independent journalists are asking questions the corporation can't erase. Emotional beat: mourning fused with momentum.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Months later, an tribunal convenes—too late, too partial, but real. Hazel testifies with the children beside her, no longer invisible. The guilty are named, though not all punished; the record, at least, can no longer be rewritten. Emotional beat: imperfect justice, fiercely claimed.

chapters.title: Dreaming in Two Languages
chapters.summary: Hazel stays on Meridian's Rest as the colony rebuilds around remembrance instead of denial. She dreams now in both tongues—human and otherwise—and teaches the children that memory is a language you keep alive by speaking it. Final beat: grief transmuted into continuity, love outlasting duty.
